description: Dark rock grown through with ice: a crown, a mouthful, bladed arms, and more torn out of the ground at need.
lore: Above the snow line the ground turns to crystal and stays that way. Nothing up there is warm long enough to become anything else, and almost nothing lives on it, and those turn out to be one fact rather than two. It is not that the high country goes untold, either. It is told constantly and by accident: every account of anything at all up there restates that it is cold, that it is high, and that it is where it was, and it has been restated in that shape by everyone who ever fell, in every language they fell with, without one of them meaning to be maintaining anything.

This is what walks about in it. The rock came first — dark, plated, heavy, no different from the ground it stood out of — and the ice is what the place did to the rock afterwards. It did not stop at the surface. Blades stand off the skull in a crown, off the shoulders, off the backs of the forearms, and the mouth is a row of them. When it wants more than it is wearing it reaches down and takes it, because up there the ground is the same material as the thing standing on it, and there has never once been a shortage.

The chips that come off it are near-black glass with a cold blue sheen, which is an odd thing to be picking up at that height. It is the stuff of the black ground far below that has no business being warm and is. People who have stood on both say the only difference is what got to the rock first, and then talk about something else. The same seam accounts for the eyes, which unsettle people rather more than the size does: a dull red spark down in one socket, no fellow to it in the other, holding steady from every angle you can take. Get a proper look at a broken one and the unsettling stops. The red is a thread in the rock and not a light behind it, and the sockets have no back to them — two holes in a face-shaped stone, about as deep as a thumb, and then solid.

The hard piece in it is not ice either. Grey plated rock with a single bright cyan seam driven through it, pocket-sized and thoroughly unpleasant to keep in a pocket: the whole creature in small, the two materials and the joint between them. What it lends is both at once. Worked into an edge it puts the cold in ahead of the metal, and whatever took the blow spends a while afterwards moving as though the ground had gone knee-deep.

It will still be standing up there when the low country it has never once visited has gone soft twice over. There is nothing in it that could be pleased about that. It has no round to walk, and nothing it is late for, and no name it keeps failing to produce; it goes where the ice is, and comes back, and has been doing that since before the first fires were lit. People who work the high ground say they do not find it frightening. They find it restful, which is its own sort of warning, and after a season of it they come down.
